prompt: A sine wave has an RMS voltage of 1 V. What changes when you replace it with an arbitrary music signal at the same RMS level?

options.text: The peak must remain exactly 1.414 V
options.explanation: The square-root-of-two relationship belongs to a sine wave.

options.text: The peak can differ, so headroom must be checked from the actual waveform
options.explanation: Correct. RMS alone does not determine peak voltage for arbitrary signals.

options.text: RMS becomes the maximum permitted input voltage
options.explanation: RMS describes a signal, not the receiving device’s rating.

options.text: The receiver no longer needs headroom
options.explanation: Music transients can still overload the receiving stage.

workedExample:
1. RMS describes a waveform’s average squared voltage after taking the square root. It does not uniquely describe its peaks.
2. A sine wave has a peak about 1.414 times its RMS value; a symmetric square wave has equal peak magnitude and RMS.
3. Other waveforms can place short peaks higher still, so leave headroom and inspect the actual waveform instead of applying the sine-only factor universally.

link.title: Root mean square and waveform crest factors
